note: S120g — predict-only, batch of eighteen. Every lesson already runs a lab clearing manipulation, consequence and misconception; only the commitment was missing. Widgets are asserted byte-identical by the converter. Each wrong option is a documented misconception the lab refutes on the spot.

predict.prompt: The vector ⟨3, 4⟩ has components 3 and 4. Its LENGTH will be…
predict.reveal: 5, by Pythagoras. The components are the two legs of a right triangle, not pieces to be totalled. Adding them measures a journey along the grid lines; the vector's length is the straight line cutting across.

predict.prompt: You walk u = ⟨3, 4⟩ first, then v, and must finish at (7, 1). The v you need is…
predict.reveal: ⟨4, −3⟩: 3 + 4 = 7 and 4 + (−3) = 1. Addition is component-wise, so the second leg is the destination MINUS wherever the first leg already took you. The negative is not a special case — it is simply the part of the journey that heads back down.

predict.prompt: A unit vector has length exactly 1. How many different unit vectors are there in the plane?

options.label: Infinitely many — one for every direction

predict.reveal: Infinitely many, all sitting on the circle of radius 1. "Unit" fixes the length and says nothing whatever about the way it points — which is exactly why v = |v|·û splits a vector cleanly into those two independent facts.

predict.prompt: log_b(8) = 3 asks: which base, cubed, gives 8? The base is…
predict.reveal: 2, because 2³ = 8. A logarithm normally hands back the exponent; here the exponent was handed to you and the base was the unknown — the same equation read from a third side. 8 ÷ 3 is what division would give, and nothing here was a division.

predict.prompt: log_b(81) = 4 asks which base raised to the FOURTH power gives 81. The base is…
predict.reveal: 3, since 3⁴ = 81. The 9 is tempting because 9² = 81 — but that is the base whose SQUARE is 81, and the ring is set at 4, not 2. Move the ring and the same 81 hands back a different base entirely.

predict.prompt: log_b(32) = 5. Before sliding anything, the base must be…
predict.reveal: 2, since 2⁵ = 32. Worth noticing what change-of-base would have said: log 32 / log b = 5, so log b = (log 32)/5 — the same base, reached through base 10 instead. Two routes, one answer, which is the whole claim the formula makes.

predict.prompt: e ≈ 2.71828. Adding terms of 1 + x + x²/2! + x³/3! + … at x = 1, getting within 0.01 of e will take…
predict.reveal: About six. The factorials in the denominators grow far faster than xⁿ can at x = 1, so each new term is a small fraction of the one before and the partial sums close in fast. That collapse is the reason a polynomial can stand in for a transcendental function at all.

predict.prompt: 1 + x + x² + … at x = 0.5 climbs toward 2. After each new term, the distance still remaining to 2 will…

options.label: Shrink by the same fixed amount each time
Barely change — it takes dozens of terms

predict.reveal: It halves. After n terms the leftover is exactly (0.5)ⁿ, so every term closes half of whatever gap is left — which is why six terms suffice. Geometric convergence is not merely getting closer; it is taking a fixed FRACTION of the remaining distance every time.

predict.prompt: 3 + 4i is plotted as the point (3, 4). Its modulus — its distance from the origin — is…
predict.reveal: 5. The modulus is Pythagoras applied to the real and imaginary parts, exactly as a vector's length is Pythagoras applied to its components. 3 + 4i and ⟨3, 4⟩ are the same arrow in different notation, and the modulus is where that stops being a metaphor.

predict.prompt: Multiplying by i turns a point through 90°. So the z whose product with i is −4 + 3i must have modulus…
predict.reveal: 5. |i| = 1, so multiplying by i cannot change any length — it only turns. That is De Moivre in a single move: moduli multiply and arguments add, so a factor of modulus 1 is pure rotation and nothing else.

predict.prompt: r = a + 2cos θ has an inner loop. Raising a will close that loop to a single cusp when a reaches…

options.label: 2 — matching the coefficient of cos θ

predict.reveal: a = 2, where the ratio a/b hits 1. The loop exists only while r can go negative; at a = 2 the smallest r is exactly 0, reached at one angle alone — and a single point where the curve touches the origin is precisely a cusp. Past 2, r never reaches zero and the shape dimples instead.

predict.prompt: A sequence starts at 3 and its 6th term must be 23. The step you need is…
predict.reveal: 4. Getting from the 1st term to the 6th is FIVE hops, not six: 3 + 5×4 = 23. Counting the terms instead of the gaps between them is the most reliable way to land one step out, and it is why the formula carries (n − 1) rather than n.

predict.prompt: 2 + 2r + 2r² + … The ratio that makes the forever-sum come to exactly 10 is…
predict.reveal: 0.8. The sum is 2/(1 − r), so a total of 10 needs 1 − r = 0.2. Notice how close to 1 the ratio must climb to pile up five times the first term — and that r = 5 is not merely the wrong value, it is outside the range where a forever-sum exists at all.

predict.prompt: The inner machine multiplies rates by 3; the outer multiplies by 5. The rate transmitted from one end of the chain to the other is…

options.label: 5 — the outer machine has the last word

predict.reveal: 15. Rates along a chain MULTIPLY — each stage scales whatever the previous one handed it, so tripling then quintupling is fifteen-fold. That single fact is the chain rule; dy/dx = dy/du · du/dx is bookkeeping laid over it.

predict.prompt: f(x) = |x| has no derivative at x = 0. The reason is that…

options.label: The function is not defined there
The slope from the left and the slope from the right disagree

predict.reveal: They disagree — −1 from the left, +1 from the right — and a limit that returns two answers returns none. |x| is perfectly defined and perfectly continuous at 0. Differentiability is the stronger promise, and this is exactly where it fails while continuity survives.

predict.prompt: p is the distance from the vertex to the focus. Sliding p LARGER makes the parabola…

options.label: The same shape, just moved up

predict.reveal: Wider. The curve is x² = 4py, so a larger p divides x² by more and flattens it. The focus rising and the parabola opening out are one event, not two: the directrix drops by the same p, and every point on the curve stays equidistant from both.

predict.prompt: A 400-person poll carries a margin of about ±5 points. To reach about ±1 point you would need roughly…
predict.reveal: About twenty-five times — some 10,000 people. The margin shrinks with the SQUARE ROOT of the sample, so cutting it to a fifth costs 5² = 25 times the sample. That is why national polls stop near a thousand: the next point of precision is ruinously expensive.

predict.prompt: This time the two methods differ by only 0.6. When you rebuild the chance pile, gaps of 0.6 or more will turn up…

options.label: Often — chance alone produces gaps this big

predict.reveal: Often, and that IS the verdict. A p-value asks what fraction of chance-produced gaps reach as far as the one you actually saw; when that fraction is large, your gap is unremarkable. Note what this does not say: not that the methods are identical, only that this evidence cannot tell them apart.
